title: Concurrency correctness
points: Correctness in concurrency means preventing data corruption when multiple threads access shared state.
The danger only exists when state is both shared between threads and mutable; if either is missing, no synchronization is needed.
Synchronization is a trade-off: every mechanism adds overhead, makes some threads wait, or adds complexity, so pick the lightest one that protects the invariant.
trade: Correctness comes first, then throughput. Start from what you are protecting (one variable or an invariant over several) and how much contention you expect. Related: race conditions (check-then-act, read-modify-write) are the bugs, and the lock/atomic/confinement concepts are the fixes.
test: A service keeps a counter in a field but every request thread only reads it and it is never changed after startup. Do you need a lock, and why?
answer: No. State that is shared but immutable cannot be corrupted, so no synchronization is needed.

questions.question: When is synchronization NOT needed?
options: When state is shared and mutable but updates are rare
When there is no shared mutable state, e.g. data is immutable or thread-local
When the machine has only a few cores
When the code uses a database
questions.explanation: Corruption needs shared AND mutable state. Rare updates (the first option) still race; core count doesn't remove the interleaving risk.

questions.question: What does 'correctness' mean in concurrent code?
options: The code runs faster with more threads
Shared state is never corrupted when threads access it at the same time
Every thread finishes in the same order it started
questions.explanation: Correctness is about protecting shared state from corruption. Speed and non-blocking are performance goals that often trade against it.
